evaluation_claims.text: Rust is a mixture of iron oxides ranging in color from red-orange to reddish-brown.
Rust consists of iron(III) oxide (Fe2O3), hydrous ferric oxides (Fe2O3·nH2O), and iron(III) oxide-hydroxide (FeO(OH)).
Rusting is an electrochemical redox reaction in which oxygen is the oxidizing agent and iron is the reducing agent.
Rusting requires both air or oxygen and liquid water or moisture.
On an iron surface with a water droplet, oxidation occurs at the center of the droplet where iron acts as the negative terminal and each iron atom gives up two electrons to form Fe2+ ions.
Electrons flow to the positive site at the droplet edge, where dissolved oxygen is reduced to hydroxide ions.
Iron(II) ions and hydroxide ions combine to form iron(II) hydroxide, which is oxidized by atmospheric oxygen to hydrated iron(III) oxide, i.e., rust.
Corrosion prevention methods aim to eliminate oxygen and water or alter the electrochemical environment.
Barrier protection places a physical shield between iron and its environment.
Paint, varnish, oil, waxes, plastic, or metal foils keep water and air from contacting iron.
Powders such as epoxy, nylon, and urethane can be adhered to a surface to form a thin protective film.
In modern paint systems, a primer coat acts as an inhibitor, an intermediate coat builds thickness, and a finish coat repels external environmental factors.
Moisture control, such as waterproof coatings or desiccants like silica gel, helps prevent rust by minimizing moisture exposure.
Rust converters are mixtures based on tannic or phosphoric acid that combine with rust to form a stable layer ready for painting.
Sacrificial protection attaches a more reactive metal, such as zinc or magnesium, to iron.
In cathodic protection, active corrosion sites are converted into passive sites by supplying electrons from another source, typically galvanic anodes of metals such as aluminum, magnesium, or zinc.
The attached sacrificial metal is more reactive, so it corrodes before the iron.
Galvanization coats iron or steel with a thin protective layer of zinc.
Zinc coating acts both as a physical barrier against oxygen and water and as a sacrificial layer.
Hot-dip galvanizing immerses iron or steel in a bath of molten zinc.
Anodic protection controls corrosion by making the metal surface the anode of an electrolytic cell.
Alloying iron with other metals, most notably chromium and nickel, increases its resistance to rust.
Stainless steel is the most common example of rust-resistant alloying.
Rust has a much higher volume than the original iron from which it forms.
Rust jacking is a failure in which expanding rust pushes adjacent structural parts apart.
In 1983, rust jacking caused the collapse of the Mianus River bridge when rust built up inside the bearings and displaced a corner of the road slab off its support.
Unlike aluminum, copper, or tin, which form protective stable oxide layers, surface rust on iron is flaky and friable and provides no passivational protection.
Any mass of iron exposed to water and oxygen can eventually convert entirely to rust.
Alloyed steel is effective against corrosion but very expensive.

Sacrificial anodes are consumed over time, requiring inspections and replacements that raise maintenance costs, add weight to structures, and are not always effective in high-resistivity environments.

reference_verifications.rationale: Wikipedia states rust is a mixture of iron oxides ranging from red-orange to reddish-brown.
Chemical composition listed exactly as stated.
Electrochemical process; iron is reducing agent, oxygen oxidizing agent; redox reaction.
Evidence says rusting needs air and water/moisture and oxygen with moisture.
Transcript says the center of the water droplet has oxidation, at the negative terminal each iron atom gives up two electrons to become Fe2+.

Electrons flow to the positive terminal where dissolved oxygen is reduced to hydroxide; 'edge of the droplet' is supported by the area on the edge of metal having reduction process, though the wording is about the metal area at the edge.
Iron(II) combines with hydroxide to form iron(II) hydroxide, which is oxidized by atmospheric oxygen to hydrated iron(III) oxide (rust).
Evidence says methods aim to keep iron from contact with water and oxygen; the 'alter the electrochemical environment' part is only loosely supported (e.g., cathodic/anodic protection).
Barrier protection uses physical barriers/coatings between iron and the environment.
Paint, varnish, oil, plastic, metal foils, and waxes keep water and air away from iron.
Evidence says powders including epoxy, nylon, urethane adhere to metal surface to create a thin film (barrier coating).
Directly states primer as inhibitor, intermediate adds thickness, finish provides resistance to environmental factors.
Keeping surfaces dry, waterproof coatings and desiccants like silica gel reduce rust likelihood.
Wikipedia text matches nearly verbatim.
Sacrificial protection described as attaching/using a more reactive metal such as magnesium or zinc with iron.
Evidence states active sites are converted to passive sites by providing electrons from another source, typically galvanic anodes of aluminum, magnesium, or zinc.
Evidence says attaching a more reactive metal means it corrodes before the iron.
Galvanization is coating iron or steel with a thin layer of zinc.

Evidence supports the barrier role (keeps water and oxygen away) and the sacrificial role (zinc corrodes preferentially), but no single source states both together; this is inferred by combining sources.
Hot-dip galvanizing is explicitly described as immersing iron or steel in a bath of molten zinc.
Evidence states anodic protection is a method to control corrosion of a metal surface by making it an anode of an electrolytic cell.
Evidence says iron can be alloyed with chromium, nickel, etc. to increase resistance against rust.
Evidence says the common example of alloying is stainless steel; 'most common' is a slight paraphrase.
Wikipedia states rust has a much higher volume than the originating mass of iron.
Evidence describes failure by forcing apart adjacent parts, known as rust jacking.
Evidence says rust jacking caused the 1983 Mianus River bridge collapse when bearings rusted internally and pushed a corner of the slab off its support.
Directly stated.
Evidence says given sufficient time any iron mass with water and oxygen forms rust and could eventually convert entirely.
Evidence says alloyed steel is among the most effective methods but very expensive.
Evidence says anodes get used up and need checking/replacing, driving up maintenance costs, add weight, and aren't always effective in high-resistivity environments.

quality.coverage_rationale: All aspects are covered. The electrolyte role is the main gap, and the inward-corrosion mechanism is only implicit.
quality.relevance_rationale: Nearly all content answers the question. The rust jacking and bridge example is a mild tangent but illustrates why rust matters. Anodic protection and rust converters are extra but related.
quality.narration_rationale: The script has a clear opening and roadmap, defines terms, and steps through the mechanism and then the prevention methods. It gives a real example in the Mianus bridge collapse. It ends with a synthesis and a reflective question. A few dense lists and LaTeX notation make it slightly less natural to read aloud.
